problems.stem: The Module 5 studio asks you to assemble a full evaluation brief. What makes the assembled brief coherent rather than a stack of separate parts?
options: Each part is long and detailed.
The evaluation question, evidence, equity check, cost, fit matrix, and recommendation all point to the same decision and support one another.
Every section uses the same template heading.
The brief includes the maximum number of tools considered.
problems.explanation: A capstone brief is coherent when its parts are linked: the recommendation answers the original question, and the evidence, equity, cost, and fit sections each justify that answer. Disconnected sections do not make a decision.

problems.stem: In assembling your brief, the cost section favors Tool A but the equity section flags that Tool A excludes students without devices. What does a strong synthesis do with this tension?
options: Hide the equity finding so the brief reads cleanly.
Surface the tension explicitly and explain which consideration was prioritized and why, so the trade-off is visible.
Average the two sections into one score.
Drop whichever section is harder to defend.
problems.explanation: Synthesis is not erasing conflict. A defensible capstone names the tension between sections and shows the reasoned choice, so a reader can see and contest the trade-off.

problems.stem: You ask an AI tool to assemble your whole Module 5 brief from your notes. It returns a complete, fluent document. What is the responsible move?
options: Submit it; the studio asked for a complete brief.
Use it as a draft, then verify that every claim traces to your own evidence and that the recommendation is one you can defend.
Ask the AI to also grade the brief.
Trust the AI assembly because it is internally consistent.
problems.explanation: A fluent AI assembly can introduce claims you never verified and a recommendation you cannot defend. The studio assesses your judgment, so each part must be grounded in your own evidence before you own the brief.

problems.stem: A reviewer notes that your finished brief is polished and complete but never states what evidence would change the recommendation. Why does this weaken the capstone?
options: A complete brief never needs a reversal condition.
A defensible decision names what could overturn it; without that, the brief presents a conclusion as fixed rather than evidence-based.
Reviewers should not ask about evidence after completion.
Polish already demonstrates the reasoning is sound.
problems.explanation: Evidence-based decisions remain open to disconfirming evidence. A brief that cannot say what would change its mind is asserting a position, not documenting a judgment that can be inspected and revised.
